claim: Bats have increased longevity compared to other mammals.
source: Bats have unique characteristics compared to other mammals, including increased longevity and higher resistance to cancer and infectious disease.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of bats in the abstract, supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Bats have higher resistance to cancer compared to other mammals.
source: Bats have unique characteristics compared to other mammals, including increased longevity and higher resistance to cancer and infectious disease.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of bats in the abstract, with supporting citations in the introduction (Seluanov et al., 2018).

claim: Bats have higher resistance to infectious disease compared to other mammals.
source: Bats have unique characteristics compared to other mammals, including increased longevity and higher resistance to cancer and infectious disease.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of bats in the abstract, with supporting citations in the introduction (Wang et al., 2011).

claim: Bat cells showed higher expression levels of Complex I components of electron transport chain (ETC).
source: Bat cells showed higher expression levels of Complex I components of electron transport chain (ETC), but, remarkably, a lower rate of oxygen consumption.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics and proteomics data presented in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Bat cells have a lower rate of oxygen consumption compared to human cells.
source: Bat cells showed higher expression levels of Complex I components of electron transport chain (ETC), but, remarkably, a lower rate of oxygen consumption.
evidence: This is supported by oxygen consumption rate measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Complex II activity may be low or reversed in bat cells, similar to an ischemic state.
source: Computational modeling interpreted these results as indicating that Complex II activity may be low or reversed, similar to an ischemic state.
evidence: This is based on computational flux modeling results and metabolomics data showing succinate accumulation.

claim: An ischemic-like state of bats was supported by decreased levels of central metabolites in bat cells.
source: An ischemic-like state of bats was also supported by decreased levels of central metabolites and increased ratios of succinate to fumarate in bat cells.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data presented in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: An ischemic-like state of bats was supported by increased ratios of succinate to fumarate in bat cells.
source: An ischemic-like state of bats was also supported by decreased levels of central metabolites and increased ratios of succinate to fumarate in bat cells.
evidence: This is supported by metabolomics data showing succinate-to-fumarate ratio was much higher in PaLung cells (5.44±0.67) compared to WI-38 cells (1.07±0.012) (p<0.001), as shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Ischemic states tend to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source: Ischemic states tend to produce reactive oxygen species (ROS), which would be incompatible with the longevity of bats.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ischemic states.

claim: Bat cells had higher antioxidant reservoirs (higher total glutathione and higher ratio of NADPH to NADP) despite higher mitochondrial ROS levels.
source: However, bat cells had higher antioxidant reservoirs (higher total glutathione and higher ratio of NADPH to NADP) despite higher mitochondrial ROS levels.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 5.

claim: Bat cells were more resistant to glucose deprivation compared to human cells.
source: In addition, bat cells were more resistant to glucose deprivation and had increased resistance to ferroptosis, one of the characteristics of which is oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by cell culture experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Bat cells had increased resistance to ferroptosis.
source: In addition, bat cells were more resistant to glucose deprivation and had increased resistance to ferroptosis, one of the characteristics of which is oxidative stress.
evidence: This is supported by ferroptosis experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Flight is an energy-intensive process that requires high metabolic rates and ATP production.
source: For example, flight is an energy-intensive process that requires high metabolic rates and ATP production (Thomas and Suthers, 1972; Maina, 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Resistance to cancer depends on multiple factors such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) management, DNA repair, and the ability to efflux genotoxic compounds.
source: Resistance to cancer depends on multiple factors such as reactive oxygen species (ROS) management, DNA repair (Huang et al., 2016; Huang et al., 2019), and the ability to efflux genotoxic compounds (Koh et al., 2019), all of which have metabolic underpinnings.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Metabolic rates of bats during flight have been documented to be approximately three times greater than basal metabolic rates in other mammals of similar size.
source: Metabolic rates of bats during flight (ATP production) have been documented to be approximately three times greater than basal metabolic rates in other mammals of similar size (Thomas and Suthers, 1972).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: In most mammalian species, increased ATP production creates increased production of ROS in the mitochondria.
source: In most other mammalian species, increased ATP production also creates increased production of ROS in the mitochondria, which can eventually lead to DNA and cellular damage (Buffenstein et al., 2008), and activate inflammasome responses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: Low amounts of ROS are a part of homeostasis and have been linked to beneficial effects on survival in multiple contexts.
source: On the other hand, low amounts of ROS are a part of homeostasis and have been linked to beneficial effects on survival in multiple contexts (Mittler, 2017; Di Meo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Different studies have proposed lower hydrogen peroxide production as a mechanism of ROS tolerance or antioxidant defense in bats.
source: Different studies have proposed different mechanisms of ROS tolerance or antioxidant defense in bats including lower hydrogen peroxide production (Brunet-Rossinni, 2004; Brunet-Rossinni and Austad, 2004; Podlutsky et al., 2005; Ungvari et al., 2008), improved DNA repair (Foley et al., 2018), higher expression of heat shock proteins (Chionh et al., 2019) and/or a drug efflux factor, ABCB1 (Koh et al., 2019), and positive selection for efficient mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: Improved DNA repair has been proposed as a mechanism of ROS tolerance or antioxidant defense in bats.
source: Different studies have proposed different mechanisms of ROS tolerance or antioxidant defense in bats including lower hydrogen peroxide production (Brunet-Rossinni, 2004; Brunet-Rossinni and Austad, 2004; Podlutsky et al., 2005; Ungvari et al., 2008), improved DNA repair (Foley et al., 2018), higher expression of heat shock proteins (Chionh et al., 2019) and/or a drug efflux factor, ABCB1 (Koh et al., 2019), and positive selection for efficient mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: Higher expression of heat shock proteins has been proposed as a mechanism of ROS tolerance or antioxidant defense in bats.
source: Different studies have proposed different mechanisms of ROS tolerance or antioxidant defense in bats including lower hydrogen peroxide production (Brunet-Rossinni, 2004; Brunet-Rossinni and Austad, 2004; Podlutsky et al., 2005; Ungvari et al., 2008), improved DNA repair (Foley et al., 2018), higher expression of heat shock proteins (Chionh et al., 2019) and/or a drug efflux factor, ABCB1 (Koh et al., 2019), and positive selection for efficient mitochondria.
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: P. alecto is a member of the Pteropodidae family and is among the largest fructivore bats in the world.
source: P. alecto is a member of the Pteropodidae family and is among the largest fructivore bats in the world.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species.

claim: P. alecto has a lifespan of over 20 years.
source: It has a lifespan of over 20 years and is documented to co-exist with lethal zoonotic viruses like Hendra and Nipah viruses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species.

claim: P. alecto is documented to co-exist with lethal zoonotic viruses like Hendra and Nipah viruses.
source: It has a lifespan of over 20 years and is documented to co-exist with lethal zoonotic viruses like Hendra and Nipah viruses.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the species.

claim: Transcriptomics detected a total of 21,952 mRNA transcripts in bat PaLung cells.
source: Transcriptomics detected a total of 21,952 mRNA transcripts in bat PaLung cells and 58,830 transcripts in human WI-38 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct result from the transcriptomics experiment.

claim: Transcriptomics detected 58,830 transcripts in human WI-38 cells.
source: Transcriptomics detected a total of 21,952 mRNA transcripts in bat PaLung cells and 58,830 transcripts in human WI-38 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct result from the transcriptomics experiment.

claim: Differential expression analysis yielded a total of 6247 transcripts that passed cutoff thresholds (|log fold change| ≥ 1 and FDR < 0.05).
source: This method yielded a total of 6247 transcripts that passed our cutoff thresholds (|log fold change| ≥ 1 and FDR < 0.05, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis, shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis identified respiratory electron transport as upregulated in PaLung cells.
source: The genes belonging to both oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) (Figure 1C) and response to hypoxia (Figure 1D) gene sets had increased transcriptional expression in PaLung cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Gene set enrichment analysis identified cellular response to hypoxia as upregulated in PaLung cells.
source: The genes belonging to both oxidative phosphorylation (OxPhos) (Figure 1C) and response to hypoxia (Figure 1D) gene sets had increased transcriptional expression in PaLung cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation and response to hypoxia are conventionally active under opposing conditions (high oxygen for OxPhos vs low oxygen for hypoxia).
source: This was interesting because, conventionally, these two pathways are active under opposing conditions (high oxygen for OxPhos vs low oxygen for hypoxia), and so would not be expected to vary in concert with each other.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these pathways.

claim: Mitochondrial proteomics profiling detected a total of 1469 proteins that had peptides detected with high confidence in both species.
source: Profiling detected a total of 1469 proteins, that had peptides detected with high confidence in both species.
evidence: This is a direct result from the proteomics experiment.

claim: 405 proteins were differentially expressed between WI-38 and PaLung cells in the proteomics analysis.
source: When we performed DE analysis on the 1469 proteins (see Materials and methods, Figure 2A), 405 were differentially expressed between WI-38 and PaLung cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis of proteomics data.

claim: 127 core mitochondrial proteins were differentially expressed between WI-38 and PaLung cells.
source: Of these 405 proteins, we identified 127 to be core mitochondrial proteins (as defined by MitoCarta and IMPI datasets), that were differentially expressed between WI-38 and PaLung cells (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis of proteomics data.

claim: Most of the 127 differentially expressed mitochondrial proteins are upregulated in bat PaLung samples (109), with very few downregulated proteins (18).
source: We observed that most of these 127 DE mitochondrial proteins are upregulated in bat PaLung samples (109), with very few downregulated proteins (18), suggesting increased mitochondrial activity in PaLung cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential expression analysis of proteomics data, shown in Figure 2B.

claim: GSEA of proteomics data identified citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation as enriched in PaLung cells.
source: Supplementary file 5 shows that PaLung mitochondria were enriched for proteins in respiratory electron transport compared to WI-38 cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The gene set for Complex I biogenesis was significantly enriched in PaLung cells in the proteomics data.
source: In particular, the gene set for Complex I biogenesis (Figure 2E) was significantly enriched in PaLung cells.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA results shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The oxygen consumption rate (OCR) under basal conditions was lower in PaLung cells compared to WI-38 cells.
source: Unexpectedly, the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) under basal conditions was lower in PaLung cells compared to WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Bat cells have much lower maximal respiratory capacity compared to WI-38 cells, indicated by FCCP treatment.
source: Notably, bat cells have much lower maximal respiratory capacity compared to WI-38 cells, indicated by FCCP treatment (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by Seahorse measurements shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The GSEA-flagged upregulation in OxPhos was driven mostly by the upregulation of Complex I subunits, for both the proteomic and transcriptomic data.
source: Taking a closer look at the omics results, we observed that the GSEA-flagged upregulation in OxPhos was driven mostly by the upregulation of Complex I subunits, for both the proteomic and transcriptomic data (Figure 2G, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the GSEA results shown in Figures 2G and 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Computational flux modeling suggests that Complex II of the ETC may run in reverse in PaLung cells.
source: When the PaLung and WI-38 models were simulated under these two constraints, the flux histograms for PaLung cells had shifted to very low or negative flux values for Complex II (Supplementary file 9).
evidence: This is based on computational flux modeling results.

claim: Complex II is also called succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) and is part of both the TCA cycle and the ETC.
source: Complex II is also called succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) and is part of both the TCA cycle and the ETC.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Complex II.

claim: SDH generally catalyzes the conversion of succinate into fumarate, accompanied by a reduction of the endogenous Quinone pool.
source: SDH generally catalyzes the conversion of succinate into fumarate, accompanied by a reduction of the endogenous Quinone pool.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SDH function.

claim: SDH has been documented to catalyze the reverse reaction, converting fumarate to succinate, although this is unconventional.
source: However, SDH has also been documented to catalyze the reverse reaction, converting fumarate to succinate, although this is unconventional.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about SDH function.

claim: An unconventional ETC paradigm where Complex I proceeds forward but Complex II proceeds in reverse has been observed in murine retinal tissues under ischemic or hypoxic conditions.
source: Such an unconventional ETC paradigm where Complex I proceeds forward but Complex II proceeds in reverse (toward the accumulation of succinate) has been observed in other systems, e.g., in murine retinal tissues (Bisbach et al., 2020) and human hearts (Chouchani et al., 2014), under ischemic or hypoxic conditions.
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: An unconventional ETC paradigm where Complex I proceeds forward but Complex II proceeds in reverse has been observed in human hearts under ischemic or hypoxic conditions.
source: Such an unconventional ETC paradigm where Complex I proceeds forward but Complex II proceeds in reverse (toward the accumulation of succinate) has been observed in other systems, e.g., in murine retinal tissues (Bisbach et al., 2020) and human hearts (Chouchani et al., 2014), under ischemic or hypoxic conditions.
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: Mass spectrometry-based targeted metabolomics resulted in the absolute quantification of 116 metabolites from central carbon metabolism.
source: Mass spectrometry-based targeted metabolomics was performed on both PaLung and WI-38 cell lines, resulting in the absolute quantification of 116 metabolites from central carbon metabolism (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment.

claim: The ratio of succinate-to-fumarate was much higher in PaLung cells (5.44±0.67) compared to WI-38 cells (1.07±0.012) (p<0.001).
source: As predicted by our hypothesis, metabolomics showed that the ratio of succinate-to-fumarate was much higher in PaLung cells (5.44±0.67) compared to WI-38 cells (1.07±0.012) (p<0.001), consistent with succinate accumulation in PaLung cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The ratio of other serial TCA metabolites, e.g., citrate/succinate or fumarate/malate, showed only mild or insignificant differences between PaLung and WI-38 cells.
source: In contrast, the ratio of other serial TCA metabolites, e.g., citrate/succinate or fumarate/malate, showed only mild or insignificant differences between PaLung and WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment, shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Previous studies have documented SDH phenomena (with the low or reverse activity of Complex II) during ischemic/hypoxic states that had low metabolic rates and high levels of AMP.
source: Interestingly, previous studies have documented such SDH phenomena (with the low or reverse activity of Complex II) during ischemic/hypoxic states that had low metabolic rates and high levels of AMP (Chouchani et al., 2014; Bisbach et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: Most metabolites from glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway, TCA cycle, and amino acids were at much lower levels in PaLung cells compared to WI-38 cells, except for a small subset of metabolites in glycolysis.
source: Looking at metabolites from glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway, TCA cycle, and the levels of amino acids, we found that most metabolites were at much lower levels in PaLung cells compared to WI-38 cells, except for a small subset of metabolites in glycolysis (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment, shown in Figures 4A-C.

claim: PaLung cells had a much higher proportion of AMP compared to WI-38 cells.
source: PaLung cells also had a much higher proportion of AMP (Figure 4D), which would be expected in an ischemic setting.
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PaLung cells had a threefold lower ATP/ADP ratio compared to WI-38 cells (p<0.001).
source: Furthermore, our metabolomics dataset revealed that PaLung cells had a threefold lower ATP/ADP ratio compared to WI-38 cells (p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: ATP/ADP ratio is a golden standard for the measurement of cellular energy status.
source: ATP/ADP ratio is a golden standard for the measurement of cellular energy status, and our results suggest lower metabolism in PaLung cells.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ATP/ADP ratio.

claim: PaLung cells had lower adenylate energy charge compared to WI-38 cells (p<0.001).
source: We found that PaLung cells had lower adenylate energy charge compared to WI-38 cells (p<0.001) (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment.

claim: Metabolomics showed higher levels of intracellular lactate in WI-38 cells than in PaLung cells.
source: However, metabolomics showed higher levels of intracellular lactate in WI-38 cells than in PaLung cells, suggesting that PaLung cells could have lower glycolytic flux than WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics experiment, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: PaLung cells had lower ECAR compared to WI-38 cells.
source: Finally, we assessed glycolysis levels using a Seahorse XF Analyzer to quantify the extracellular acidification rate (ECAR). This revealed that PaLung cells had lower ECAR compared to WI-38 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a direct result from the ECAR measurement, shown in Figure 4E.

claim: PaLung cells displayed higher viability than WI-38 cells after glucose deprivation for 96 hr.
source: Interestingly, PaLung cells displayed higher viability than WI-38 cells after glucose deprivation (Figure 4F), despite starting with lower stores of internal energy (e.g. glucose-6-phosphate, acetyl-CoA, and lower adenylate charge).
evidence: This is a direct result from the glucose deprivation experiment, shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PaLung cells showed higher mitochondrial superoxide levels compared to WI-38 cells, both under basal conditions and when ETC was inhibited using antimycin A.
source: Indeed, PaLung cells showed higher mitochondrial superoxide levels compared to WI-38 cells, both under basal conditions and when ETC was inhibited using antimycin A (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a direct result from the MitoSOX assay, shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SOD1 and SOD2 are less expressed in PaLung cells than in WI-38 cells.
source: Notably, SOD1 and SOD2, key enzymes that convert mitochondrial superoxide to the more toxic intracellular ROS, are less expressed in PaLung cells than in WI-38 cells, consistent with higher mitochondrial superoxide levels in PaLung cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the transcriptomics data, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3) was found to be highly upregulated in PaLung cells compared to WI-38 cells.
source: Interestingly, glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3), a well-known antioxidant enzyme that reduces hydrogen peroxide or organic hydroperoxides using glutathione, was found to be highly upregulated in PaLung cells compared to WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the transcriptomics data, shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione (GSH/GSSG ratio) was not significantly different between PaLung and WI-38 cell lines.
source: The ratio of reduced to oxidized glutathione (GSH/GSSG ratio) was not significantly different between the two cell lines (WI-38 cells: 36.45±3.6 vs PaLung cells: 30.94±2.97).
evidence: This is a direct result from the glutathione measurement assay, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PaLung cells had a twofold higher concentration of total intracellular glutathione, compared to WI-38 cells.
source: However, PaLung cells had a twofold higher concentration of total intracellular glutathione, compared to WI-38 cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the glutathione measurement assay, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PaLung cells had a higher NADPH/NADP ratio (1.5-fold) compared to WI-38 cells.
source: We also found that PaLung cells had a higher NADPH/NADP ratio (1.5-fold) compared to WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the NADPH/NADP measurement assay, shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The metabolomics data indicated that PaLung cells had a nearly 2.5-fold higher ratio of NADP/NAD, i.e., a higher resting concentration of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated NAD.
source: Overall, the metabolomics data indicated that PaLung cells had a nearly 2.5-fold higher ratio of NADP/NAD, i.e., a higher resting concentration of phosphorylated to unphosphorylated NAD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a direct result from the metabolomics data, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Transcriptomics showed an upregulation of NADK (NAD kinase) and supporting enzymes required to synthesize and phosphorylate NAD in PaLung cells.
source: This was also supported by transcriptomics which showed an upregulation of NADK (NAD kinase) and supporting enzymes required to synthesize and phosphorylate NAD (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the transcriptomics data, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Ischemic conditions can induce cell death via ferroptosis, which depends on accumulated ROS and low glutathione levels.
source: Many earlier studies have shown that ischemic conditions can induce cell death via ferroptosis, which also depends on accumulated ROS and low glutathione levels (Chen et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citation.

claim: Ischemia-induced ferroptosis causes tissue damage and inhibition of ferroptosis attenuates ischemia-induced cell death.
source: Recent studies have reported that ischemia-induced ferroptosis causes tissue damage and that inhibition of ferroptosis attenuates ischemia-induced cell death (Xie et al., 2019; Liao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated as findings from previous studies with supporting citations.

claim: Ferroptosis is a non-apoptotic, programmed form of cell death, which is iron-dependent and occurs via glutathione depletion-induced lipid peroxidation.
source: Ferroptosis is a non-apoptotic, programmed form of cell death, which is iron-dependent and occurs via glutathione depletion-induced lipid peroxidation (Ursini and Maiorino, 2020).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citation.

claim: WI-38 cells showed high sensitivity to erastin-induced ferroptosis that were prevented by a ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1.
source: While WI-38 cells showed high sensitivity to erastin-induced ferroptosis that were prevented by a ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1, PaLung cells were resistant to erastin-induced ferroptosis (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the ferroptosis experiment, shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: PaLung cells were resistant to erastin-induced ferroptosis.
source: While WI-38 cells showed high sensitivity to erastin-induced ferroptosis that were prevented by a ferroptosis inhibitor ferrostatin-1, PaLung cells were resistant to erastin-induced ferroptosis (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is a direct result from the ferroptosis experiment, shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: PaLung cells were more resistant to cystine deprivation-induced ferroptosis, compared to WI-38 cells and had almost sevenfold lower cell death than WI-38 cells (3.5% cell death in PaLung cells compared to 24.4% cell death in WI-38 cells upon cystine deprivation).
source: Similarly, PaLung cells were more resistant to cystine deprivation-induced ferroptosis, compared to WI-38 cells and had almost sevenfold lower cell death than WI-38 cells (3.5% cell death in PaLung cells compared to 24.4% cell death in WI-38 cells upon cystine deprivation) (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is a direct result from the ferroptosis experiment, shown in Figures 6C and D.

claim: Both WI-38 and PaLung cells showed decreased GSH/GSSG ratio under cystine deprivation, which indicates both cell lines are under oxidative stress.
source: Both WI-38 and PaLung cells showed decreased GSH/GSSG ratio under cystine deprivation, which indicates both cell lines are under oxidative stress (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is a direct result from the glutathione measurement under cystine deprivation, shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Cystine deprivation decreased total glutathione levels in WI-38 cells by 94.5%, nearly depleting glutathione reserves.
source: Cystine deprivation decreased total glutathione levels in WI-38 cells by 94.5%, nearly depleting glutathione reserves.
evidence: This is a direct result from the glutathione measurement under cystine deprivation, shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Cystine deprivation in PaLung cells resulted in only a modest 29.5% decrease in total glutathione, and PaLung cells still maintained a total glutathione level higher than non-cystine-deprived WI-38 cells.
source: In contrast, cystine deprivation in PaLung cells resulted in only a modest 29.5% decrease, and PaLung cells still maintained a total glutathione level higher than non-cystine-deprived WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is a direct result from the glutathione measurement under cystine deprivation, shown in Figure 6F.

claim: This is the first comprehensive analysis combining proteomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, and constraint-based flux modeling between human and bat cells.
source: Although data are still limited to these two cell lines, this is the first comprehensive analysis combining proteomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, and constraint-based flux modeling between human and bat cells.
evidence: This is stated as a claim about the novelty of the study.

claim: PaLung cells exhibit basal metabolism that resembles an ischemic-like state.
source: Our analysis suggests that PaLung cells exhibit basal metabolism that resembles an ischemic-like state and that this state may be linked to low or reverse activity of Complex II of the ETC (also called SDH).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence including metabolomics, computational modeling, and functional assays.

claim: Compared to WI-38 cells, PaLung cells show a higher tolerance to cellular stresses such as nutrient deprivation.
source: Compared to WI-38 cells, PaLung cells also show a higher tolerance to cellular stresses such as nutrient deprivation and ischemia/ROS-driven cell death via ferroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4F and 6.

claim: Compared to WI-38 cells, PaLung cells show a higher tolerance to ischemia/ROS-driven cell death via ferroptosis.
source: Compared to WI-38 cells, PaLung cells also show a higher tolerance to cellular stresses such as nutrient deprivation and ischemia/ROS-driven cell death via ferroptosis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Hypoxia response (including glycolysis) and OxPhos compensate for each other by gene expression, dependent on different levels of oxygen availability.
source: Hypoxia response (including glycolysis) and OxPhos compensate for each other by gene expression, dependent on different levels of oxygen availability.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these pathways.

claim: Lactate production in PaLung cells was not higher than in WI-38 cells.
source: Although multiple glycolytic genes were upregulated in PaLung cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), lactate production (inferred via both LDH expression levels and ECAR measurement) in PaLung cells was not higher than in WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is based on transcriptomics data and ECAR measurements shown in Figures 1—figure supplement 2 and 4E.

claim: ECAR depends only on the amount of lactate produced, and glycolytic pyruvate that enters the TCA cycle may remain invisible to ECAR measurements.
source: This raises an important caveat about using ECAR to infer glycolytic flux, because ECAR depends only on the amount of lactate produced, and glycolytic pyruvate that enters the TCA cycle may remain invisible to ECAR measurements.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological consideration about ECAR measurements.

claim: The succinate-to-fumarate ratio in well-oxygenated PaLung cells was found to be similar to those found in ischemic states of human cells from multiple tissues.
source: The succinate-to-fumarate ratio in well-oxygenated PaLung cells was found to be similar to those found in ischemic states of human cells from multiple tissues (Chouchani et al., 2014).
evidence: This is based on comparison of metabolomics data with published literature.

claim: PaLung cells highly express glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3).
source: On the other hand, PaLung cells highly express glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3), contain twofold higher levels of glutathione, and maintain a higher NADPH/NADP ratio compared to WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is based on transcriptomics data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PaLung cells contain twofold higher levels of glutathione compared to WI-38 cells.
source: On the other hand, PaLung cells highly express glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3), contain twofold higher levels of glutathione, and maintain a higher NADPH/NADP ratio compared to WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is based on glutathione measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PaLung cells maintain a higher NADPH/NADP ratio compared to WI-38 cells.
source: On the other hand, PaLung cells highly express glutathione peroxidase 3 (GPX3), contain twofold higher levels of glutathione, and maintain a higher NADPH/NADP ratio compared to WI-38 cells.
evidence: This is based on NADPH/NADP measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The previously published generalization that bats have lower free radical production than other mammals may require moderation.
source: Therefore, the previously published generalization that bats have lower free radical production than other mammals (Brunet-Rossinni, 2004; Brown et al., 2009) may require moderation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding of higher mitochondrial ROS in PaLung cells.

claim: Multiple studies have shown strong links between ischemia, ROS, and ferroptosis.
source: Multiple studies have shown strong links between ischemia, ROS, and ferroptosis (an iron-dependent, non-apoptotic form of cell death).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Ferroptosis occurs via ROS-induced lipid peroxidation following ischemia and is conventionally blocked via the action of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4).
source: Ferroptosis occurs via ROS-induced lipid peroxidation following ischemia and is conventionally blocked via the action of glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about ferroptosis.

claim: GPX4 expression levels were low in PaLung cells.
source: While GPX4 expression levels were low in PaLung cells, GPX3 (a commonly secreted form of glutathione peroxidase) was highly expressed.
evidence: This is based on transcriptomics data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: GPX3 (a commonly secreted form of glutathione peroxidase) was highly expressed in PaLung cells.
